newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF meeting seen key to Pakistani stock outlook.
newsitem.headline: IMF meeting seen key to Pakistani stock outlook.

text.p: A meeting of Pakistani and IMF officials in Washington this week could decide the near-term fate of the troubled Pakistani stock market, possibly preventing a major slide, dealers said on Monday.
But political and economic uncertainty still kept the overall outlook for the market gloomy, they added.
"We are in for a bumpy ride," dealer Ali Asghar at Fortune Securities said.

A Pakistani delegation led by V.A. Jafarey, finance adviser to Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, is to meet International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials this week in an effort to convince them to resume a stalled $600 million standby loan.
The IMF has delayed payment of a $80 million tranche of the standby loan, which was due for delivery in June, pending a review of Pakistan's budget for 1996/97 (July-June).

"Failing to get a positive reply from the IMF, the market is likely to tumble to a new year-low and may keep falling if the political situation does not improve," dealer Hina Akhlaq of KASB & Co said.

The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index, which hit a record low last November of 1323.53, ended on Monday down 6.58 points at 1,385.17. It has lost a hefty 25 percent since a 1996 peak in mid-February.
Dealers said concerns over Pakistan's wide trade deficit, high inflation and falling reserves have weighed on the market, while fresh political uncertainty has shaken confidence.

On September 20, the prime minister's estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto and seven aides were killed in a shootout with police in Karachi. The market has since tumbled, sliding 3.7 percent since September 21.
Murtaza's followers accused police of ambushing and killing their leader deliberately. But the police say they shot in self-defence after being fired at by Murtaza's bodygaurds.

An apparent feud between the prime minister and President Farooq Leghari over powers to make judicial appointments and how to fight corruption has also raised concerns over the future of Bhutto's nearly three-year-old government.
The market received another shock last Tuesday after U.S.-based Moody's Investors Service Inc placed Pakistan's credit rating under review for possible downgrading.

"At the moment most of the major players have adopted a wait-and-see approach. The market is unlikely to take a definite direction until the IMF meeting clears up the situation," dealer Salman Iqbal said.
He said Pakistan was in a dire need of IMF help while its credit rating remains under review, adding that an estimated $700 million worth of debt repayments were due in October.
"As the perception of the political situation gets worse, only a positive news from the economic front can halt a major slide to new lows," Akhlaq from KASB & Co said.
At the moment the only good news for the market could come from the IMF, he added.
The ouster of President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government in neighbouring Afghanistan by the Taleban Islamic movement had little impact on Pakistan's markets, the dealers added.
